sentences.t:
Him se yldesta andswarode,
werodes wīsa, wordhord onlēac:
sentences.l: To him the eldest answered, the troop's leader, unlocked the word-hoard:
sentences.i: The eldest of them answered him; the leader of the band unlocked his store of words:
sentences.n: ‘Him’ is a dative, since ‘andswarode’ (‘answered’) takes the dative of the one answered; the speech answers the coast guard's questions at 237–257. ‘se yldesta’ is the superlative of ‘eald’, ‘old’, so ‘the eldest’; it may mean oldest in years or highest in rank, and the next phrase, ‘werodes wīsa’, ‘leader of the troop’, points to rank. ‘wīsa’ comes from the same stem as ‘wīsade’ ‘showed the way’ (208). ‘wordhord onlēac’ is ‘unlocked the word-hoard’. A ‘hord’ is a stored treasure, and the kenning sets speech in the breast like gold in a chest that the speaker opens. The poem uses it for a man beginning to speak. The speaker is not named in these lines.

sentences.t:
‘Wē synt gumcynnes Gēata lēode
ond Higelāces heorðgenēatas.
sentences.l: ‘We are of mankind Geats' people and Higelac's hearth-companions.
sentences.i: ‘We are men of the Geat people, and Higelac's hearth-companions.
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb besides ‘synt’ (‘are’); ‘Gēata lēode’ and ‘heorðgenēatas’ are both predicates, joined by ‘ond’. ‘gumcynnes’ is a genitive, ‘of the race of men’. Its force here is a guess: it may be a plain filler meaning ‘human folk’, or it may mark origin, ‘by birth’. ‘Gēata lēode’ is ‘people of the Geats’, with ‘lēode’ the plural of ‘lēod’. ‘heorðgenēatas’ is ‘hearth-companions’: ‘heorð’ is the hearth and ‘genēat’ is one who shares in something, so these are retainers who share their lord's fire and table. Higelāc is the man named at 194 as the lord of the Geat hero (‘Higelāces þegn’). The speaker gives his people and his lord and does not yet give his own name.

sentences.t:
Wæs mīn fæder folcum gecȳþed,
æþele ordfruma, Ecgþēow hāten;
sentences.l: Was my father to the peoples made known, a noble front-founder, called Ecgþēow;
sentences.i: My father was known among the peoples, a noble chief, called Ecgþēow;
sentences.n: ‘Wæs … gecȳþed’ is a passive, ‘was made known’, with ‘folcum’ in the dative plural, ‘to peoples’. ‘hāten’ is the participle of ‘hātan’, ‘to call, name’, and ‘Ecgþēow hāten’ is ‘called Ecgtheow’. Klaeber's apparatus lists several editors who think line 262 incomplete and add a word ([monegum], [foldan], [frōd], [feor]); Klaeber prints none, and the sentence makes sense without one. ‘ordfruma’ joins ‘ord’, ‘point, front, beginning’, with ‘fruma’, ‘beginning, founder’. ‘Chief’ is a guess at the compound's sense, from the picture of a man at the spear-point or head of a people. The name ‘Ecgþēow’ is probably ‘ecg’, ‘sword-edge’, and ‘þēow’, ‘servant’. The speaker names his father before himself.

sentences.t:
gebād wintra worn, ǣr hē on weg hwurfe,
gamol of geardum;
sentences.l: he lived-through a multitude of winters, before he away turned, old, from the yards;
sentences.i: he lived through many winters before he departed, an old man, from the dwellings of men;
sentences.n: ‘gebād’ is the past tense of ‘gebīdan’, here ‘lived through, experienced’, and ‘wintra worn’ is ‘a multitude of winters’: ‘wintra’ is a genitive plural, and Old English counts years in winters. ‘ǣr hē on weg hwurfe’ is ‘before he turned away’, with ‘hwurfe’ a past subjunctive, the mood ‘ǣr’ takes for an event that had not yet happened while the winters were passing. ‘On weg hweorfan’ is a soft way to say ‘to die’. ‘gamol of geardum’ is ‘old, out of the yards’; a ‘geard’ is an enclosure, a dwelling-place, and ‘of geardum’ takes the reading ‘from the dwellings (of the living)’, which is an interpretation.

sentences.t:
hine gearwe geman
witena wēlhwylc wīde geond eorþan.
sentences.l: him well remembers of wise-men each, widely throughout the earth.
sentences.i: every wise man, far and wide over the earth, remembers him well.
sentences.n: ‘hine’ is the accusative object of ‘geman’, ‘remembers’, a present tense; Ecgþēow is dead and the memory continues. ‘witena wēlhwylc’ is ‘each one of the counsellors’: ‘witena’ is a genitive plural of ‘wita’, a wise man who advises kings, and ‘wēlhwylc’ means ‘each one’; some lexica give ‘almost every’, taking ‘wēl’ as ‘nearly’, so the force is ‘each’ or ‘nearly all’. ‘gearwe’ is ‘well, fully’, the adverb Fitt III has at 246 for ‘clearly’. ‘wīde geond eorþan’ is ‘widely throughout the earth’.

sentences.l: We through a loyal mind your lord, the son of Healfdene, to seek came, people-protector;
sentences.i: We have come in loyalty to seek your lord, the son of Healfdene, protector of his people;
sentences.n: The core is ‘Wē … sēcean cwōmon’, ‘we came to seek’, with the infinitive ‘sēcean’ stating the purpose. ‘þurh holdne hige’ is ‘through a loyal mind’, meaning ‘with loyal intent’. ‘hlāford’ is the accusative object of ‘sēcean’, and ‘þīnne’ is ‘your’ because the coast guard is Hrothgar's man; ‘sunu Healfdenes’ and ‘lēodgebyrgean’ stand beside it and name the same king: he is Healfdene's son and the one who shelters the people. ‘lēodgebyrgea’ is built from ‘lēod’, ‘people’, and ‘gebeorgan’, ‘to protect’; the sense ‘protector of the people’ follows from the parts and is a guess about a rare word. ‘hlāford’ is our ‘lord’, from ‘hlāf-weard’, ‘loaf-keeper’.

sentences.t: wes þū ūs lārena gōd!
sentences.l: be you to us of counsels good!
sentences.i: be good to us with your counsel!
sentences.n: ‘wes’ is the imperative of ‘wesan’, ‘be’, and ‘þū’ is ‘you’. ‘ūs’ is a dative, ‘to us’, and ‘lārena’ is a genitive plural, ‘of counsels’, which depends on ‘gōd’: ‘be good to us in respect of counsel’. The speaker asks the coast guard for guidance in how to proceed.

sentences.t:
Habbað wē tō þǣm mǣran micel ǣrende
Deniga freân;
sentences.l: Have we to the famed one a great errand, the Danes' lord;
sentences.i: We have a great errand to the famous lord of the Danes;
sentences.n: ‘Habbað wē’ puts the verb first, ‘have we’. ‘tō þǣm mǣran … Deniga freân’ is ‘to the famed lord of the Danes’; ‘Deniga’ is a genitive plural of ‘Dene’, ‘Danes’, and the circumflex in ‘freân’ is Klaeber's mark for a contracted vowel, here the dative singular of ‘frēa’, ‘lord’. ‘ǣrende’ means ‘errand’ or ‘message’, and the line does not settle which; they have business with the king and also something to tell him. The ‘lord of the Danes’ is Hrothgar, whose name appears at 277.

sentences.t:
ne sceal þǣr dyrne sum
wesan, þæs ic wēne.
sentences.l: not shall there secret any be, of that I expect.
sentences.i: nothing there shall be secret, as I expect.
sentences.n: ‘ne sceal … wesan’ is ‘shall not be’, and ‘dyrne sum’ is ‘anything hidden’ (‘dyrne’ is ‘secret’, and ‘sum’ here is an indefinite ‘some’). ‘þæs ic wēne’ is ‘of this I expect’: ‘þæs’ is a genitive of the thing believed, and ‘wēne’ is the first person of ‘wēnan’, ‘to expect, think’. ‘þǣr’ is ‘there’, in the matter of the errand; the clause is read here as a promise that the errand has nothing to hide, a guess from context.

sentences.t:
Þū wāst, gif hit is
swā wē sōþlīce secgan hȳrdon,
þæt mid Scyldingum sceaðona ic nāt hwylc,
dēogol dǣdhata deorcum nihtum
ēaweð þurh egsan uncūðne nīð,
hȳnðu ond hrāfyl.
sentences.l: You know, if it is so as we truly say heard, that among the Scyldings, of ravagers I know-not which, a secret deed-hater on dark nights shows through terror an unknown malice, injuries and corpse-fall.
sentences.i: You know whether it is as we have truly heard it said, that among the Scyldings some ravager, I cannot say who, a lurking doer of hateful deeds, shows on dark nights, by terror, a strange hostility, injuries and carnage.
sentences.n: ‘Þū wāst’ is ‘you know’, the present of ‘witan’. The clause ‘gif hit is swā wē … hȳrdon’ (‘if it is as we heard’) is slipped in before the thing known, which is given after ‘þæt’: ‘þæt … ēaweð’, ‘that … shows’. ‘ic nāt hwylc’ is ‘I know not which’, from ‘ne wāt’, and ‘sceaðona’ is a genitive plural, so the phrase means ‘one of the ravagers, I know not which’. The visitors have heard of the attacks and cannot say who makes them; a reader of Fitt II knows he is Grendel. ‘dēogol’ is ‘secret, hidden’. ‘dǣdhata’ is ‘deed-hater’, ‘one who hates by deed’; the sense is a guess, and the apparatus records an alternative form, ‘dǣdhwata’ (Klu.), with a different second element (‘hwata’, a rare word). ‘deorcum nihtum’ is a dative of time, ‘on dark nights’. ‘ēaweð’ (‘shows’) has three objects: ‘uncūðne nīð’ (‘unknown malice’, with ‘nīð’ as hostility), ‘hȳnðu’ (‘injuries, humiliations’) and ‘hrāfyl’ (‘corpse-fall’, with ‘hrā’ a dead body and ‘fyl’ a falling or killing). ‘egsan’ is ‘terror’, an accusative after ‘þurh’.

sentences.t:
Ic þæs Hrōðgār mæg
þurh rūmne sefan rǣd gelǣran,
hū hē frōd ond gōd fēond oferswȳðeþ —
sentences.l: I in this Hrothgar can through a roomy mind counsel teach, how he, wise and good, the enemy overcomes —
sentences.i: From a generous mind I can advise Hrothgar in this, how he, wise and good, may overcome the enemy —
sentences.n: ‘Ic … mæg … gelǣran’ is ‘I can teach’, and the verb takes both the person taught and the thing taught in the accusative: ‘Hrōðgār’ is the one taught (the form is not a dative, which would end in -e) and ‘rǣd’, ‘counsel’, is what he is taught. ‘þæs’ is a genitive, ‘in this matter’. ‘þurh rūmne sefan’ is ‘through a roomy mind’, meaning ‘with a generous, open spirit’. ‘hū hē … oferswȳðeþ’ is an indirect question, ‘how he overcomes’, a present tense that English renders with ‘may’ or ‘will’ because it speaks of a hope. ‘frōd ond gōd’ is ‘wise and good’; ‘frōd’ also carries the sense of age. Hrōðgār is the king of the Danes, son of Healfdene, as in Fitt I. The dash opens an aside that finishes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
gyf him edwenden ǣfre scolde
bealuwa bisigu bōt eft cuman —,
sentences.l: if for him reversal ever should, of evils the trouble, remedy again come —,
sentences.i: if ever a turning for the better should come for him, a remedy again for the affliction of those evils —
sentences.n: ‘gyf … scolde … cuman’ is ‘if ... should come’, and the subject is ‘edwenden’, ‘a turning back, reversal’, with ‘bōt’, ‘remedy’, beside it as a second word for the same thing. ‘him’ is a dative, ‘for him’, meaning Hrothgar. ‘bealuwa bisigu’ is ‘the trouble of evils’; ‘bealuwa’ is a genitive plural of ‘bealu’, and ‘bisigu’ is a form of ‘bisgu’, ‘busy-ness, affliction’. Its case is not certain here; the phrase is read as the affliction that the remedy answers. The italic ‘e’ in ‘edwenden’ is Klaeber's sign that he changed the manuscript: both 1787 transcripts (A, B) read ‘edwendan’, and Klaeber prints ‘edwenden’, as the apparatus shows Bugge (‘Bu.’), Holthausen (‘Holt.’) and Sedgefield (‘Sed.’) read it, which makes the word a noun with the ending -en. The dash and comma together close the aside.

sentences.t: ond þā cearwylmas cōlran wurðaþ;
sentences.l: and those care-surges cooler become;
sentences.i: and those surges of care grow cooler;
sentences.n: This clause finishes the question that began with ‘hū’ at 279: ‘how he may overcome the enemy and the care-surges grow cooler’. ‘wurðaþ’ is the plural present of ‘weorðan’, ‘to become’, matching the plural subject; the apparatus records that some editors prefer an infinitive, ‘wurðan’ or ‘weorðan’, which would put the clause inside the ‘if’ before it. ‘cearwylmas’ is ‘care-surges’ (‘cearu’, ‘sorrow’, and ‘wylm’, ‘boiling, welling-up’), another heat-picture for grief, like the seething of Hrothgar at 189 in Fitt III. The comparative ‘cōlran’ means ‘cooler’.

sentences.t:
oððe ā syþðan earfoðþrāge,
þrēanȳd þolað, þenden þǣr wunað
on hēahstede hūsa sēlest.’
sentences.l: or ever afterwards a hardship-time, dire need he suffers, while there remains on the high place of houses the best.’
sentences.i: Or else he will go on suffering a time of hardship and bitter need, for as long as the best of houses stays there on its high place.’
sentences.n: ‘oððe’ is ‘or’, and sets a second possibility beside the cure just named. The subject (Hrothgar) is not stated; ‘þolað’ has the same form in the singular and the plural, and the singular is taken here. ‘ā syþðan’ is ‘ever afterwards’. ‘earfoðþrāge’ joins ‘earfoþ’, ‘hard’, with ‘þrāg’, ‘time’ (as in ‘longe þrāge’, ‘for a long time’, at 54 in Fitt I); ‘a hard time’ is the sense, a guess for a rare compound. ‘þrēanȳd’ is ‘distress-need’. ‘þolað’ is ‘suffers’. ‘þenden’ means ‘while’, and ‘wunað’ ‘remains’. ‘on hēahstede’ is ‘on the high place’, and ‘hūsa sēlest’ is ‘the best of houses’ (‘hūsa’ is a partitive genitive plural). The house is the hall of Fitt I, Heorot. The closing mark ends the elder's speech.

sentences.t:
Weard maþelode, ðǣr on wicge sæt,
ombeht unforht:
sentences.l: The guardian spoke in speech-words, where on his horse he sat, an officer unafraid:
sentences.i: The watchman spoke in formal words, there where he sat on his horse, a fearless officer:
sentences.n: ‘Weard’ is ‘guardian’, the coast guard of 229, and ‘maþelode’ is the verb ‘to speak’ in set words; the noun form was ‘meþelwordum’ at 236, where the translation has ‘formal words’. The poem introduces a formal reply this way, and the speech-words here are the answer. ‘ðǣr on wicge sæt’ is ‘there on his steed he sat’; ‘wicg’ is a horse. ‘ombeht’ is ‘officer, servant’, a word borrowed from Celtic, related to German ‘Amt’, and ‘unforht’ is ‘unafraid’, so ‘fearless officer’ names the same man as ‘Weard’. The colon opens a new speech.

sentences.t:
‘Ǣghwæþres sceal
scearp scyldwiga gescād witan,
worda ond worca, sē þe wēl þenceð.
sentences.l: ‘Of each of two must the sharp shield-warrior distinction know, of words and of works, he who well thinks.
sentences.i: ‘A keen shield-warrior who thinks well must know how to discern each of the two, words and deeds alike.
sentences.n: ‘Ǣghwæþres’ is a genitive, ‘of each of two’, and line 289 explains the two: ‘worda ond worca’, ‘of words and of works’, both genitive plural. ‘sceal … witan’ is ‘must know’, and ‘gescād’ is ‘discernment, a dividing’. ‘scearp scyldwiga’ is ‘sharp shield-warrior’, ‘sharp’ in the sense of keen-minded. ‘sē þe wēl þenceð’ is ‘he who thinks well’, naming the same man again. The guard is saying that a good soldier judges visitors by what they say and what they do.

sentences.t:
Ic þæt gehȳre, þæt þis is hold weorod
frēan Scyldinga.
sentences.l: I that hear, that this is a loyal troop to the lord of the Scyldings.
sentences.i: I understand that this is a company loyal to the lord of the Scyldings.
sentences.n: ‘gehȳre’ is ‘I hear, I take it’; the first ‘þæt’ points ahead, and the clause after the second ‘þæt’ is ‘þis is hold weorod’, ‘this is a loyal troop’. ‘frēan Scyldinga’ is a dative, ‘to the lord of the Scyldings’, and ‘hold’ takes the dative: loyal to Hrothgar. ‘hold’ is the adjective of ‘holdne’ at 267, where the elder claimed loyalty for the same errand.

sentences.t:
Gewītaþ forð beran
wǣpen ond gewǣdu, ic ēow wīsige;
sentences.l: Go forth to bear weapons and garments, I you will guide;
sentences.i: Go forward bearing your weapons and gear, and I will lead you;
sentences.n: ‘Gewītaþ’ is the plural imperative of ‘gewītan’, ‘go’, and ‘forð beran’ is ‘forth to bear’, so ‘go on, carrying’. ‘wǣpen ond gewǣdu’ is ‘weapons and garments’, the second word meaning clothing, including mail. ‘ic ēow wīsige’ is ‘I will guide you’; ‘wīsige’ is a first-person present, a form that serves for both indicative and subjunctive, and it gives the guard's intention. ‘wīsige’ is from ‘wīsian’, ‘to show the way’, the verb at 208.

sentences.t:
swylce ic maguþegnas mīne hāte
wið fēonda gehwone flotan ēowerne,
nīwtyrwydne nacan on sande
ārum healdan, oþ ðæt eft byreð
ofer lagustrēamas lēofne mannan
wudu wundenhals tō Wedermearce,
gōdfremmendra swylcum gifeþe bið,
þæt þone hilderǣs hāl gedīgeð.’
sentences.l: Likewise I my youth-thanes command against every one of foes your ship, the newly-tarred boat, on the sand with honor to guard, until again bears over the water-streams the dear man the wound-necked wood to the Weder-march, of good-doers to such a one it is granted, that that battle-onrush whole he comes through.’
sentences.i: I will also order my young thanes to guard your ship against every enemy, your newly tarred boat there on the sand, and to keep it with honor until the curved-necked timber carries the beloved man back over the sea-currents to the land of the Weders; to any such man among those who do good it is granted to come unharmed through the onrush of battle.’
sentences.n: This is one long sentence, and the cut comes at the closing quote. ‘swylce’ is ‘likewise, also’. The main clause is ‘ic maguþegnas mīne hāte … healdan’, ‘I order my young thanes to guard’ (present ‘hāte’, ‘I command’, an order given now). ‘maguþegnas’ joins ‘magu’, ‘son, young man’, to ‘þegn’, ‘thane’; ‘young thanes’ is the sense taken here, a guess (the literal line says ‘youth-thanes’). The objects are ‘flotan ēowerne’ and ‘nacan’, two words for the ship (‘flota’ is ‘floater’; ‘naca’ is ‘boat’), and ‘wið fēonda gehwone’ is ‘against every one of foes’. ‘nīwtyrwydne’ occurs nowhere else; ‘newly tarred’, from ‘nīwe’, ‘new’, and the stem of ‘tyrwa’, ‘tar’, is a guess. ‘ārum’ is a dative plural of ‘ār’, ‘honor, favor’, so ‘with honor’. ‘oþ ðæt eft byreð’ is ‘until it bears again’, and the subject is ‘wudu wundenhals’, ‘wound-necked wood’: the ship, with ‘wundenhals’ (‘wound’ is twisted, ‘hals’ neck) a guess for a prow that curves like a neck; Fitt III has ‘wundenstefna’ (220) for the same picture. Its object is ‘lēofne mannan’, ‘the dear man’, a singular that may stand for their leader or for each of the company, which is a choice. ‘lagustrēamas’ are ‘water-streams’. ‘Wedermearce’ is ‘Weder-march’, the Weders' land; ‘Wederas’ is another name for the Geats, as in ‘Wedera lēode’ at 225. In the last two lines ‘gōdfremmendra swylcum’ is ‘to such a one of good-doers’, and ‘gifeþe bið’ is ‘it is granted’. ‘hilderǣs’ is ‘battle-rush’, and ‘gedīgeð’ ‘comes through’. The apparatus records that ‘Gru.’ and others read ‘gūðfremmendra’, ‘war-doers’, as at 246, instead of ‘gōdfremmendra’, ‘good-doers’.

sentences.t:
Gewiton him þā fēran, — flota stille bād,
seomode on sāle sīdfæþmed scip,
on ancre fæst.
sentences.l: Went themselves then to go, — the floater waited still, rode on its rope, the broad-bosomed ship, fast at anchor.
sentences.i: Then they set off on their way; the ship stayed quietly where it was, riding on its rope, the broad-bosomed vessel, held fast by its anchor.
sentences.n: ‘Gewiton him þā fēran’ is ‘went themselves then to travel’, built like ‘Gewāt him … rīdan’ at 234: ‘him’ is a reflexive dative and ‘fēran’ an infinitive after a verb of motion. The dash sets the next clause alongside the going. ‘flota’ is the ship, ‘floater’, as at 210; ‘stille’ is ‘still’, and ‘bād’ is ‘waited, stayed’. ‘seomode on sāle’ is ‘rode at its rope’ (‘lay at rest’), from ‘seomian’, ‘to lie at rest’, with ‘sāl’ a rope: the italic ‘ā’ is Klaeber's sign that he changed the manuscript, which reads ‘sole’; an earlier editor (‘E.Sc.’ in the apparatus) put ‘sāle’. ‘sīdfæþmed’ is ‘broad-bosomed’ (‘sīd’, ‘wide’; ‘fæþm’, ‘embrace, bosom’), a guess at ‘roomy’. ‘on ancre fæst’ is ‘fast at anchor’.

sentences.t:
Eoforlīc scionon
ofer hlēorber[g]an gehroden golde,
fāh ond fȳrheard, — ferhwearde hēold
gūþmōdgum men.
sentences.l: Boar-forms shone over the cheek-guards, adorned with gold, shining and fire-hard, — life-guard held for the war-minded man.
sentences.i: Boar-images shone above the cheek-guards, adorned with gold, bright and hardened in fire, and kept watch over the life of the war-hearted man.
sentences.n: This unit is full of guesses. ‘Eoforlīc’ is ‘boar-image’ (‘eofor’, ‘boar’; ‘līc’, ‘form’); the figures are on the visitors' helmets, and a boar on a helmet is usually understood as a guard for its wearer. ‘scionon’ is read as the past plural of ‘scīnan’, ‘to shine’; the apparatus records other editors who take it as a noun (‘scīone’, ‘līcscīonon’), so the verb is not settled. ‘ofer hlēorber[g]an’ is ‘over the cheek-guards’ (‘hlēor’, ‘cheek’; ‘beorg’, ‘protection’). The bracketed ‘g’ is Klaeber's addition: the manuscript has ‘beran’, and he follows ‘E.’ and Gering (as the apparatus abbreviates them) in making ‘hlēorbergan’ of it. ‘gehroden golde’ is ‘adorned with gold’. ‘fāh’ is ‘gleaming’ or ‘variegated’, and ‘fȳrheard’ ‘fire-hard’, from a fire-tempering, which is a guess for a word found only here. The dash sets off a second statement about the boar-images, ‘ferhwearde hēold’, whose singular verb follows the plural ‘scionon’, one more oddity in the passage. ‘ferhwearde’ may be ‘life-guard’ (‘ferh’, ‘life, spirit’; ‘weard’, ‘guard’), which is taken here as a guess. The apparatus gives other readings: ‘fearh’ (‘pig’, ‘boar’) as the first part, or ‘færwearde’. The last words are the roughest. The manuscript has ‘guþmod grummon’, where ‘grummon’ is not a word; Kemble and others read ‘gūðmōd[e] grummon’, from ‘grimman’, ‘to rage’, and Bugge made ‘gūþmōdgum men’ of it, the form Klaeber adopts. The italic ‘gu’ in ‘gūþmōdgum’ and ‘e’ in ‘men’ mark where he changed the manuscript. ‘gūþmōdgum men’ is therefore a guess: a dative, ‘to the war-minded man’, in which ‘men’ stands for the helmeted warrior or the company together.

sentences.l: Men hastened, marched together, until they the hall timbered, splendid and gold-gleaming, could perceive;
sentences.i: The men hurried on, marching together, until they could make out the timbered hall, splendid and shining with gold;
sentences.n: ‘Guman ōnetton’ is ‘men hastened’, from ‘ōnettan’; ‘sigon ætsomne’ is ‘they moved together’, with ‘sigon’ the past plural of ‘sīgan’, ‘to sink, move steadily’. ‘oþ þæt hȳ … ongyton mihton’ is ‘until they could perceive’; ‘hȳ’ is a spelling of ‘hīe’, ‘they’, and ‘ongyton’ the plural past of ‘ongietan’. The object, ‘[s]æl timbred’, is ‘the timbered hall’ (‘sæl’, ‘hall’; ‘timbred’, ‘built of timber’). The bracketed ‘s’ is Klaeber's: the manuscript runs the words together as ‘æltimbred’, and Kemble supplied the ‘s’. ‘geatolīc ond goldfāh’ is ‘splendid and gold-gleaming’ (‘fāh’ as at 305). The hall is Heorot, which Fitt II named (166) but this passage does not.

sentences.t:
þæt wæs foremǣrost foldbūendum
receda under roderum, on þǣm se rīca bād;
sentences.l: that was foremost to earth-dwellers of halls under the skies, in which the mighty one dwelt;
sentences.i: that was the most renowned of halls under the heavens to all who live on earth, the one in which the mighty king dwelt;
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is the hall seen at 307–308. ‘foremǣrost’ is ‘most famous’ (‘mǣre’ is ‘famed’, and ‘fore-’ marks the front rank), and ‘foldbūendum’ is a dative, ‘to earth-dwellers’ (‘folde’ is earth, ‘būend’ one who lives), a compound that names humankind. ‘receda’ is a genitive plural, ‘of halls’, and ‘under roderum’ is ‘under the heavens’ (‘rodor’ is the sky). ‘on þǣm se rīca bād’ is ‘in which the powerful one stayed’; ‘bād’ is the past of ‘bīdan’, ‘to wait, remain’, as at 301. ‘se rīca’ is the king, Hrothgar.

sentences.t: līxta se lēoma ofer landa fela.
sentences.l: gleamed the light over lands many.
sentences.i: its radiance shone over many lands.
sentences.n: ‘līxta’ is the past tense of ‘līxan’, ‘to gleam’, and ‘lēoma’ is a ray or radiance, here the light the hall gives off, after ‘goldfāh’ (308). ‘ofer landa fela’ is ‘over many lands’: ‘fela’ takes a genitive plural, ‘landa’.

sentences.l: To them then the battle-brave one the court of the proud ones bright pointed out, that they to it straight could go;
sentences.i: Then the warrior brave in battle showed them the bright court of the proud men, so that they could go straight to it;
sentences.n: ‘Him’ is a dative, ‘to them’, and ‘hildedēor’ is ‘battle-brave’ (‘hilde’, ‘battle’; ‘dēor’, ‘bold’): the coast guard, who is the subject of ‘getǣhte’, ‘showed, pointed out’. ‘[h]of mōdigra’ is ‘the court of the proud’. The bracketed ‘h’ is Klaeber's: the manuscript has ‘of’, and Kemble added the ‘h’, giving ‘hof’, ‘dwelling, court’; the genitive plural ‘mōdigra’ is ‘of the high-spirited ones’, meaning the king and his men. ‘torht’ is ‘bright’, and it is read here with ‘hof’. ‘þæt hīe him tō mihton gegnum gangan’ is ‘so that they could go straight to it’: ‘him’ is ‘to it’ and ‘gegnum’ is ‘directly’.

sentences.t:
gūðbeorna sum
wicg gewende, word æfter cwæð:
sentences.l: one of the war-men turned the steed, a word afterwards said:
sentences.i: One of the warriors turned his horse and afterwards spoke a word:
sentences.n: ‘gūðbeorna sum’ is ‘one of the war-men’, with ‘sum’ followed by a genitive plural as in ‘fīftȳna sum’ at 207; it is read as the coast guard again, an inference from ‘hildedēor’ above, and he is the subject of ‘gewende’, ‘turned’. ‘wicg’ is the horse, ‘word æfter cwæð’ is ‘a word afterwards said’, so a parting remark as he turned to go. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.t: ‘Mǣl is mē tō fēran;
sentences.l: ‘Time is for me to go;
sentences.i: ‘It is time for me to go;
sentences.n: ‘Mǣl’ is ‘time, the right time’ (the word in ‘mǣlceare’, 189) and ‘mē tō fēran’ is ‘for me to go’.

sentences.t:
Fæder alwalda
mid ārstafum ēowic gehealde
sīða gesunde!
sentences.l: May Father all-ruler with favors keep you, safe in journeys!
sentences.i: May the Father, ruler of all, keep you in his favor, safe in your ventures!
sentences.n: ‘gehealde’ is a subjunctive of wish, ‘may he keep’, and the line is a blessing. ‘Fæder alwalda’ is ‘Father all-ruler’ (‘al-’, ‘all’; ‘walda’, ‘ruler’), an epithet of God. ‘ēowic’ is an older accusative of ‘gē’, ‘you’, the form ‘ēow’ with the ending ‘-ic’. ‘mid ārstafum’ is ‘with favors’: ‘ār’ is ‘honor, mercy’ and ‘stæf’ a staff or support, so ‘ārstafas’ are acts of kindness; this reading is built from the parts of the compound. ‘sīða gesunde’ is ‘safe as to journeys’, with ‘sīða’ a genitive plural of respect and ‘gesunde’ agreeing with ‘ēowic’. The poem's narrator is a Christian, and the guard's blessing uses the same God as the thanks at 227.

sentences.t:
Ic tō sǣ wille,
wið wrāð werod wearde healdan.’
sentences.l: I to the sea will, against a hostile troop watch to hold.’
sentences.i: I will go to the sea, to keep watch against a hostile band.’
sentences.n: ‘wille’ is ‘will, wish’, and the verb of motion is left out, as Old English allows: ‘I (will go) to the sea’. ‘wið wrāð werod’ is ‘against a hostile troop’ (‘wrāð’ is ‘angry, hostile’), and ‘wearde healdan’ is ‘to hold watch’, the same watch as ‘ǣgwearde hēold’ at 241 in the coast guard's first speech. The closing mark ends the speech. He goes back to the sea-watch he left to ride out and meet them.
